nkoren · Nov 28, 2026

Well, Soleri will come back to haunt me from beyond the grave if I let the "utopian" bit go unchallenged, and so: he hated that label. He equated "utopian" with "divorced from reality", and said that the American norm of hyperconsumption and suburban sprawl was in fact utopian. He was very serious about standing in opposition to this, and therefore considered Arcosanti's frugality to be anti utopian.

Most of the people there bought into this to one degree or another -- although apart from that most basic premise (which itself wasn't universally embraced), there wasn't a lot of agreement about anything else. While Arcosanti did exist within the general milieu of the "intentional community" movement -- and therefore pulled in a lot of people with that interest -- there was no top-down effort to foster that, and the bottom-up efforts tended to be haphazard and short-lived.

That said, there were some ways in which it was definitely a bubble apart from the rest of reality, and those ways were fun.

kragen · Nov 28, 2026

What do you think would we need to succeed at what Arcosanti attempted?

nkoren · Nov 28, 2026

In my day, if you'd asked this question to anybody at Arcosanti, they would have said "money".

That answer would have been wrong, or at least incomplete. You can draw a straight line from Soleri's late-stage "linear arcology" concept to Saudi Arabia's, well "The Line" -- which has done a fine job of proving that having more money than sense is also not an effective way to build an arcology.

The problem is/was that Arcosanti had no viable economic or governance model, nor did it even attempt to have one. It's a big vision glued to a small bell-making business and a small nonprofit foundation -- which adds up to being a small company town -- and has never made a sincere effort to be anything else. That'll just never be an effective way to build a city.

Why was it so constrained?

For Soleri: economics and governance were basically just blank spots in his philosophy. He knew that he hated capitalism in general and consumerism in specific -- but this didn't translate into wanting to seriously try any kind of alternative model. This took a lot of possibilities off the table without putting anything back on it.

For the rest of the management: transitioning away from being a small company town --however that was done -- would have required stepping far outside of an increasingly entrenched comfort zone. So they had little motivation to do so.

yepyoukno · Nov 28, 2026

Opinions are like farts in the wind. Arcosanti is what it is, having survived a world that tears everything down for not being what someone else wanted.

Modern regulation makes experiments too expensive and time expansive. It really takes ten years to see how things “turn out”, and a lot easier to let concrete settle. Decades ago there was a concert and hundreds of people’s cars parked on a field of dry grass burned up. Insurance covered it, however the regulatory crack down and insurance stipulations made their “heyday” of renegade construction impossible in today’s world. Critics often do not recognize this and other challenges.

Today you need a plan, the cash, and the permits to start day one. Arcosanti was intended as an organic growth over time in an era more optimistic and naive.

There are lessons there, some not those one might expect.
